sections.label: GSA and LTBA issuance limits
sections.summary: The GSA limit was last raised in 2016 to S$690 billion, with S$642 billion outstanding, while the LTBA's S$60 billion is fully used.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For the GSA, the last increase for the issuance limit took place in 2016, when Parliament approved the increase of the Government's issuance limit from S$490 billion to S$690 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Currently, the outstanding amount of securities issued under the GSA is S$642 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Currently, the outstanding amount of securities issued under the LTBA is S$60 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, the Government has fully utilised the prevailing LTBA limit, and we expect to utilise the prevailing GSA limit before mid this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Under the GSA, we project that the outstanding amount of securities will reach S$960 billion by the end of 2025.

sections.label: CMTB tenure under six months
sections.summary: CMTB tenure will be tailored to the period of need and be less than six months, issued solely for short-term cashflow management.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The tenure of CMTB will be tailored to meet the period of need and will be less than six months as it will be issued solely for short-term cashflow management.

sections.label: CMTB maximum size S$10 billion
sections.summary: The CMTB's maximum size is envisaged to be no larger than S$10 billion, accounted for under the proposed LTBA limit increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The maximum size of the CMTB is envisaged to be no larger than S$10 billion, which has been accounted for under the proposed increase in the LTBA borrowing limit.

sections.label: Raising Government Securities Act ceiling
sections.summary: The Motion proposes raising the GSA issuance ceiling by S$270 billion to S$960 billion, expected to last five years till 2025.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For the present Motion, I propose to raise the ceiling for issuing Government Securities under the Government Securities Act by S$270 billion to S$960 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The proposed limit of S$960 billion will apply to the outstanding amount of Government Securities and is expected to last for five years till 2025.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Under the Government Securities Act, these borrowings can only be used for investments and the proceeds are safeguarded in the Government Securities Fund.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: If the current Government runs into an end-of-term deficit, it has to either cut spending, increase revenue by raising taxes or seek consent from the President to draw on past reserves.

sections.label: Basis for lifting debt ceilings
sections.summary: The passage states the issuance and funds raised are unrelated to the country's fiscal position and asks the basis for lifting debt issuance ceilings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We know that this issuance and the funds raised are unrelated to the country's fiscal position.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: So, what are the basis and the considerations for lifting the debt issuance ceilings?

sections.label: Infrastructure, green and social bonds
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Government would consider newer issuance variations such as infrastructure, green or social bonds for special purpose funding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Would the Government also consider newer variations of issuances, such infrastructure bonds, green bonds or social bonds, for special purpose funding?

sections.label: Clarification of $270 billion figure
sections.summary: The speaker asks for clarification of the assumptions behind the $270 billion figure.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For starters, I would like to ask for some clarification over the underlying assumptions that support the specific figure of $270 billion.

sections.label: Borrowing ceiling and growth scenarios
sections.summary: The passage states that a ceiling based on pessimistic growth may be too generous or too low depending on the recession's length.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If the economy does eventually bounce back strongly – much like how it did following the SARS epidemic or even the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis – then, a ceiling premised on a more pessimistic growth trajectory may turn out to be excessively generous.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In contrast, if the recession proves to be more drawn out – akin to the aftermath of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis – then, this amount of borrowing may turn out to be insufficient to even meet routine needs, necessitating yet another round of requests to raise the ceiling.

sections.label: Low rates and fiscal spending
sections.summary: The passage states that near-zero rates make real borrowing costs negative and asks whether prudent fiscal spending should replace monetary policy.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Furthermore, in countries where rates are close to zero, positive inflation means that borrowing costs in real terms are negative.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This means that the costs of borrowing are no longer prohibitive and, perhaps, the more pertinent question is not so much whether we should incur more public debt or even how much public debt is on the books but whether in this environment of low interest rates and deficient demand, prudent fiscal spending is required to take the place of otherwise independent impotent monetary policy.

sections.label: Combined borrowing limit increase
sections.summary: The passage states that $270 billion and $45 billion limit increases bring the combined borrowing limit to $1.065 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The current round of $270 billion and $45 billion limit increases for Government Securities and Treasury Bills respectively will bring the combined borrowing limit to $1.065 trillion.

sections.label: Financial assets and Government Securities holdings
sections.summary: The passage states $1.35 trillion in financial assets as of March 2020, with Government Securities held by the public and CPF Board.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As a result, we have accumulated $1.35 trillion of financial assets as of March 2020; and with our financial assets way in excess of our liabilities, our country enjoys the Triple A Sovereign Credit Rating.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As of March 2020, about $136 billion of Government Securities is held by the public, of mainly Singaporeans and local financial institutions and $433 billion held by the CPF Board.

sections.label: Excess cash held by Statutory Boards
sections.summary: The passage states that as of March 2020, excess cash held by Statutory Boards totalled about $50 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As of March 2020, my estimate of the excess cash held by the Statutory Boards totalled about $50 billion.

sections.label: Debt, budget and tax recommendations
sections.summary: The speaker recommends using debt prudently, tightening budget allocation and reintroducing tax collection avenues, asking the Government to reconsider them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If the Government believes that we are in a new normal, then old policies and extension of them will no longer be the answer of the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I have thus made several recommendations or ask various questions on how to make use of debt prudently, tighten up budget allocation to increase financial discipline and reintroduce multiple tax collection avenues to boost our financial standing which I hope the Government will reconsider in totality.

sections.label: Debt financing for infrastructure
sections.summary: The speaker agrees there is scope for debt financing in Singapore and says borrowing for long-term major infrastructure projects is being studied.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I am in complete agreement with the broader points that are raised, that there is scope for debt financing in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And that is why we have said that we are studying very carefully the use of borrowing for long-term major infrastructure projects.

sections.label: CPF needs and SSGS issuance
sections.summary: The speaker says CPF needs are growing and almost 75% of the increase in proposed limits will be issued for SSGS for CPF needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Number one, CPF needs are growing and I have highlighted, almost 75% of the increase in the proposed limits will be issued for SSGS, for CPF needs.

sections.label: Increasing GSA and LTBA limits
sections.summary: Financial institutions have demand for these assets, limits have been reached, so increases in the GSA and LTBA are provided to issue more SGS and Treasury Bills.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, financial institutions have demand for these assets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have reached the limits and therefore we are also providing for an increase in the GSA and in the LTBA to provide to issue more SGS and the shorter term Treasury Bills.

sections.label: Sovereign debt limits and servicing
sections.summary: Statutory Board debt is governed by their legislation, while SGS and Treasury Bills limits are set in the Government Securities Act and Local Treasury Bills Act and authorised by Parliament; debt servicing is met from investment returns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The provisions, the safeguards for the issuance of debt by Statutory Boards are governed in their respective legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But, for sovereign debt, SGS, Singapore Government Securities, Treasury Bills, we have the two Acts that we are referring to today – the Government Securities Act and the Local Treasury Bills Act; and the limits for issuance of debt under these two Acts are set out in the Act and authorised by Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Mr Liang asked about borrowing cost and whether we can ensure that we are able to invest well enough to pay the debts, debts that we borrow through the Singapore Government Securities; and the answer is yes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: They are constantly looking out for long-term investment opportunities and overall, we are able to meet our debt servicing cost fully from the returns generated from our investments.

sections.label: Interest rates and negative territory
sections.summary: Singapore interest rates are determined more by global rates, which are monitored; rates are expected to stay low and not enter negative territory.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Our interest rates in Singapore are determined more by global interest rates, but we monitor this very carefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I think for now, our situation is such that we expect interest rates to remain low for quite some time until we see a broader upturn in the global economy and a normalisation of monetary policy, we do not expect to enter into negative interest rate territory.
